Bent
bent
a. and v. (drawn, as a bow made ready to shoot; used of the wicked preparing against the upright, and once, terribly, of God against Zion)
From Old English bendan, to bend a bow — the original English sense of the verb is specifically to string and draw a bow. The Hebrew is darak, to tread, since an ancient war bow was strung by setting the foot against it and treading it down.

Biblical Definition

The Hebrew verb behind bent is darak, to tread — a great bow was strung by putting the foot on it, which is why Scripture speaks of treading the bow. Two parties are shown with bows bent. The wicked: “The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, and to slay such as be of upright conversation” (Psalm 37:14) — the psalm answers three verses later that their bows shall be broken. And God Himself: “If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready” (Psalm 7:12). The conditional is the mercy in that verse; the whetting and the bending wait on if he turn not. Isaiah shows the Assyrian coming with “all their bows bent” (Isaiah 5:28), the instrument of the same judgment. The most painful occurrence is in Lamentations, where the bow is bent by the covenant God against His own city: “He hath bent his bow like an enemy: he stood with his right hand as an adversary, and slew all that were pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion” (Lamentations 2:4). Jeremiah does not soften it, and the book's great confession of mercies that are new every morning stands in the very next chapter.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines bent as incurvated, made crooked, or inclined — and notes the bow drawn and ready as the original sense.

expand to see more

BENT, pp. of bend. Incurvated; made crooked; inclined; prone; having a fixed propensity; determined.

BEND, v.t. To strain, or to crook by straining; as, to bend a bow.

2. To crook; to make crooked; to curve; to inflect.

BENT, n. The state of being curving, crooked, or inclined from a straight line.

2. Declivity; as the bent of a hill. 3. Inclination; disposition; a leaning or bias of mind.

Key Scripture

Psalm 7:12 — "If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready."

Psalm 37:14 — "The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, and to slay such as be of upright conversation."

Isaiah 5:28 — "Whose arrows are sharp, and all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs shall be counted like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind:"

Lamentations 2:4 — "He hath bent his bow like an enemy: he stood with his right hand as an adversary, and slew all that were pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion: he poured out his fury like fire."

Modern Corruption

The wrath of God is treated as an emotion unworthy of Him, so Psalm 7:12 and Lamentations 2:4 are read as ancient projection rather than revelation.

expand to see more

The standing modern objection is that a God of love could not be described bending a bow against anyone, least of all His own people, and that such texts record Israel's projection of its experience onto heaven. The doctrine of divine impassibility, rightly held, does not help that objection at all — it means God is not moved by passions as creatures are, not that He has no settled and holy opposition to sin. Scripture is unembarrassed. Lamentations 2 is an inspired poem in which the prophet says outright that the LORD stood as an adversary against Zion, and Jeremiah is not correcting a mistaken view; he is confessing a righteous judgment his people had been warned of for a century.

What must not be lost is the shape of Psalm 7:12. If he turn not — the bow is bent and the condition is stated, which is what a warning is. God announces His judgments in advance, and the announcement is itself an act of mercy; Nineveh had forty days and used them. The same book of Lamentations that says he hath bent his bow like an enemy says in the next chapter that His compassions fail not and are new every morning, and both are the voice of one man in one week. A theology that can hold only one of those sentences has not understood either.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew darak, to tread — and so to string a bow; Psalm 7:12, 37:14, Lamentations 2:4; qesheth, a bow; chets, an arrow — Isaiah 5:28.

expand to see more

Hebrew darak — to tread; used of stringing a bow by treading it, hence bent.

Hebrew qesheth — a bow; the weapon in every occurrence of the word.

Hebrew chets — an arrow; Isaiah 5:28, “whose arrows are sharp.”

Hebrew latash — to whet or sharpen; Psalm 7:12, of the sword.

Old English bendan — originally to string and draw a bow, not merely to curve.

Usage

"“He hath bent his bow, and made it ready” — and the verse begins if he turn not."

"“The wicked… have bent their bow” — and the psalm answers that it shall be broken."

"“He hath bent his bow like an enemy” — Lamentations, three verses from the new mercies."
